title: 世界の外傷危機、より賢い外傷医療の必要性を浮き彫りに
title_zh: 全球外伤危机敲响警钟：创伤救治需要更聪明的做法
lead: アフリカと南アジアの約9,000人の負傷者を対象とした研究により、退院後3か月の時点で半数近くが死亡または障害を負っていることが明らかになった。研究チームは、救急車や専門病院への搬送といった一般的な対策だけでは十分ではないと指摘している。
lead_zh: 一项针对非洲和南亚约9000名伤者的研究发现，出院三个月后仍有近半数人死亡或留下残疾。研究团队指出，光靠救护车和转送专科医院这类常见做法并不够。

paragraphs: イギリスのバーミンガム大学が中心となった国際研究チームは、アフリカと南アジアの4か国で入院した負傷者8,858人を分析した。その結果、退院後3か月以内に死亡または中等度から重度の障害を負った患者は47.6%に達した。入院中に死亡したのは6.1%、3か月以内の死亡は9.7%であり、40.6%が障害を抱えて生活していた。
研究によれば、生存と回復を左右する最大の要因は、けがそのものだけでなく、患者が医療システムの中でどのような経路をたどるかである。救急車で搬送された患者は、他の手段で来院した患者に比べて死亡または障害の可能性が86%高く、3か月以内の死亡リスクも2倍以上であった。
しかし、研究を主導したジャスティン・デイビス教授は、これは救急車が結果を悪化させるという意味ではないと説明する。救急車の体制に投資するだけでは、サービスが調整され、十分な人員と資源が確保されなければ、結果の改善は期待できないというのである。
研究チームは、富裕国の医療モデルをそのまま他の国に当てはめるべきではないと主張する。各国は自国のデータや資源、患者のニーズに基づいて外傷医療の仕組みを築くべきだという。また、近くの病院で応急処置を受けることが有益な場合もあり、専門病院が近ければ直接向かう方が良い場合もあるとしている。
世界の負傷による死亡の約90%は低・中所得国で起きており、疾病負担の約10%を占めると推定される。しかし、外傷医療は感染症や慢性疾患に比べて国際的な関心が低い。研究では、南アフリカは障害の可能性が最も低い一方で死亡の可能性が最も高く、ルワンダは死亡の可能性が最も低いなど、国による差も際立った。
研究対象者の年齢の中央値は31歳で、76.8%が男性であった。記録された負傷の50%は交通事故によるもので、整形外科的な負傷が39.2%と最も多かった。研究チームは、どのような投資が患者の結果を改善するのか、より良いデータとさらなる研究が必要だとしている。
paragraphs_zh: 以英国伯明翰大学为首的国际研究团队分析了非洲和南亚四国住院的8858名伤者。结果显示，出院后三个月内死亡或留下中重度残疾的患者高达47.6%。住院期间死亡者占6.1%，三个月内死亡者占9.7%，另有40.6%的人带着残疾生活。
研究指出，决定生存与康复的最大因素不只是伤势本身，还包括患者在医疗系统中走过的路径。乘救护车到院的患者，相比用其他方式到院的患者，死亡或残疾的概率高出86%，三个月内死亡的风险也超过两倍。
不过，主导研究的贾斯汀·戴维斯教授解释说，这并不意味着救护车会让结果变差。如果服务体系缺乏协调、人员和资源不足，仅仅投资救护车系统恐怕难以改善结果。
研究团队主张，不应把富裕国家的医疗模式直接照搬到其他国家。各国应根据本国的数据、资源和患者需求来建立外伤医疗体系。此外，先在附近医院接受应急处理有时是有益的；如果专科医院就在附近，直接前往可能效果更好。
全球约90%的受伤死亡发生在低中等收入国家，估计占疾病负担的约10%。然而，相比传染病和慢性病，外伤医疗在国际上受到的关注要少得多。研究还发现国别差异明显：南非残疾概率最低但死亡概率最高，卢旺达死亡概率最低。
研究对象年龄中位数为31岁，76.8%为男性。记录在案的伤势中，50%由交通事故造成，骨科损伤最多，占39.2%。研究团队表示，需要更好的数据和更多研究，才能弄清哪些投入真正能改善患者的结局。

A study of almost 9,000 injury patients across Africa and South Asia has found that nearly half were dead or disabled after three months—highlighting the need for smarter, locally tailored trauma-care systems.
Publishing its
findings in
The Lancet Global Health
, the international research group led by University of Birmingham experts reveals that the biggest influences on survival and recovery are not just the injuries themselves, but how people move through the health care system.
Injuries cause an estimated 4.4 million deaths annually worldwide, with 90% occurring in LMICs. This is the first large multicountry study to examine mortality and disability outcomes among hospitalized injury patients across low- or middle-income countries (LMIC).
The study reveals that access to appropriate care, the route patients take to the hospital and the type of services available all play an important role in these outcomes.
Analyzing data from 8,858 patients treated in 19 urban and rural hospitals across Ghana, Pakistan, Rwanda and South Africa, the Global Health Group on Equitable Access to Quality Health Care for Injured People in Four Low- or Middle-Income Countries (Equi-injury) reveals an enormous and often overlooked global health burden:
47.6% of patients either died or were left with moderate-to-severe disability within three months of hospital discharge.
6.1% died in the hospital, 9.7% had died within three months, and 40.6% were living with moderate-to-severe disability three months after discharge.
Patients arriving at the hospital by ambulance had significantly worse outcomes, with 86% higher odds of death or disability and more than double the odds of mortality within three months compared with those using other forms of transportation.
Lead author Professor Justine Davies, from the University of Birmingham, said, "One of our most surprising findings was that measures often assumed to improve outcomes—such as ambulance transport and rapid transfer to major hospitals, which are similar to highly centralized trauma services—were not consistently linked with better recovery or survival.
"This does not mean that ambulances cause worse outcomes but suggests that investment in ambulance systems alone is unlikely to improve outcomes unless services are coordinated and appropriately resourced."
The findings challenge assumptions that health care models developed in wealthier countries can simply be copied elsewhere. Instead, the study argues that countries should develop trauma and injury-care systems based on local evidence, resources and patient needs.
Corresponding author Dr. Leila Ghalichi, from the University of Birmingham, said, "This does not mean ambulances or specialist trauma centers are ineffective. Rather, it suggests that simply investing in expensive emergency systems is not enough.
"LMICs should be cautious about investing heavily in ambulance services and specialist, centralized trauma centers without ensuring they are well coordinated, properly staffed and supported by strong health systems. Better data and further research are needed to understand which trauma-care investments improve patient outcomes."
The study notes that stopping first at a nearby hospital for emergency stabilization may sometimes be beneficial, especially if a specialist hospital is far away. If a major trauma hospital is close by, going directly there may improve outcomes.
Researchers found no evidence that reaching a hospital more quickly reduced the risk of death. Patients who experienced some delays were less likely to be disabled later—challenging the common belief that faster treatment always leads to better outcomes after injury.
Age was linked to worse outcomes, but gender, wealth and education had little effect on survival while patients were in the hospital. However, once out of the hospital, wealthier and better-educated patients tended to recover better, suggesting that access to rehabilitation and follow-up care may play an important role.
Some 90% of global injury deaths occur in LMICs and are estimated to account for around 10% of the global burden of disease. Yet trauma care receives far less attention than infectious diseases or chronic conditions in global health policy.
Country-level differences were striking. Patients in South Africa had the lowest odds of disability but the highest odds of mortality, while patients in Rwanda experienced the lowest odds of mortality. Meanwhile, patients in Pakistan experienced substantially higher odds of the combined outcome of death or disability than those in Ghana.
The study population reflects the demographics of injury worldwide. The median age was 31 years, 76.8% were male, and road traffic collisions accounted for 50% of all injuries recorded. Orthopedic injuries were the most common injury type, affecting 39.2% of patients.
